newsitem.title: GERMANY: Daimler making sharp turnaround after record loss.
newsitem.headline: Daimler making sharp turnaround after record loss.

text.p: Daimler-Benz AG , only a year after reporting the largest loss in German corporate history, surprised investors Tuesday with the speed of its turnaround, claiming a convincing return to profits.

Speaking to reporters at the Geneva auto show, a member of the Daimler-Benz management board, Eckard Cordes, said Daimler would report group net profit of more than 2.0 billion marks ($1.2 billion) for its 1996 business year, a sharp reversal from last year's 5.7 billion mark ($3.3 billion) loss.

Cordes added that sales last year were more than 107 billion marks ($62.7 billion), up from 103.5 billion marks ($61 billion) in 1995 and revenues would grow another 5 percent this year at the company dominated by its Mercedes-Benz car division.

The two billion mark profit figure was well beyond the 1.6 billion marks to 1.8 billion marks ($940 million to $1.05 billion) that analysts had expected the company to report and fuelled expectations for yet stronger profit growth this year.
"These figures were much better than expected," said Georg Stuerzer, analyst at Vereinsbank Research in Munich. "Daimler is going in the right direction."
Daimler-Benz will not officially release its 1996 results until its annual press conference next month. A spokesman there would not confirm Cordes' statements on profits.
In financial markets, however, Cordes' remarks ignited a quick round of buying in the early hours of trading, pushing Daimler stock up more than 3.5 percent to a record high of 128.20 marks.
The higher profit comes as welcome relief for Daimler Chairman Juergen Schrempp, who has been criticised for his aggressive reorganization of the company.
It also helps vindicate the plans of former Mercedes boss Helmut Werner to embark on a historic broadening of the carmaker's line.
Analysts attributed the fast profit growth to the success of Mercedes, the benefits of painful cost-cutting measures taken last year and a stronger dollar, which has helped boost demand from abroad.
Although not all the company's critics have been silenced, the profit figures above all reflect the success of Daimler's main business line -- luxury cars made by Mercedes-Benz.

The company's workhorse E-Class model, which has been available for a full year, is selling well despite challenges from Bayerische Motoren Werke AG's new 5-series. A newly introduced SLK two-seat roadster has seen demand far exceed expectations.
Those models helped push Mercedes sales last year to 645,000 units, up from 590,200 units the year before.
Sales could climb further this year as Mercedes widens its product range to include the A-Class -- a five door hatchback designed to appeal to younger buyers.
The profit figure also reveals progress in cutting costs at aircraft unit Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG, which in 1995 was devastated by a strong mark and sagging demand in the global aircraft market.
Under Schrempp's leadership, DASA slashed its work force, cut off life-supporting funds for Fokker NV and sold Dornier Luftfahrt GmbH to American aircraft maker Fairchild.
With costs down, DASA is now poised to benefit from better times at Airbus Industrie in which it is a major stake-holder, and a pick up in the regional aircraft market.
